data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: The Bank of Mongolia targets inflation (currently around 6%) under a managed float, but the tugrik's swings and commodity dependence make for a volatile record: 28.0% in 2008, 13.8% in 2012, near zero in 2016, then 15.1% in 2022 on the Ukraine-war shock, easing to a projected 8.6% in 2025, still above target. Fiscal dominance has repeatedly undermined the central bank, notably in 2016 when off-budget spending forced a crisis. Policy has tightened credibly since the 2017 IMF program, but pass-through from tugrik depreciation remains the structural challenge.
debt_management: Public debt tracks the mining cycle: 40.9% of GDP in 2006, falling to 31.0% in the 2008-10 boom, then climbing to 86.9% in 2017 after the 2016 crisis (which included the infamous Chinggis bond splurge), before disciplined policy and the coal boom brought it to a projected 45.1% in 2025. GDP grew from $3.4bn to a projected $25.4bn. The 2017 IMF Extended Fund Facility ($5.5bn package) was the turning point, imposing fiscal rules that have broadly held. Debt is now manageable, though still sensitive to coal prices and Chinese demand.

key_events.event: Commodity boom and bust; inflation hit 28.0% then growth stalled.
Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold investment agreement signed, anchoring future growth.
Fiscal crisis: off-budget spending and falling commodity prices forced an IMF approach; debt hit 78.7%.
$5.5bn IMF-led package approved; fiscal consolidation began.
COVID-19 closed the Chinese border, hitting coal exports; debt rose to 83.4%.
Coal export boom on high prices; revenues surged and debt fell to 64.5%.
Debt projected down to 45.1% as Oyu Tolgoi underground production ramped up.

outlook_next_decade: Mongolia's base case is solid growth on copper (Oyu Tolgoi underground) and coal exports to China, with debt continuing to decline if fiscal rules hold. The structural risks are unchanged: extreme dependence on China (nearly all exports), commodity-price cycles, and the political temptation to spend windfalls. Governance of mining revenues remains the key variable. Analytical assessment: the 2017 framework works when respected; the question is whether the next boom tests it.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
